text: Signature-based and anomaly-based detection are the two fundamental ways an IDS or IPS decides something is malicious. Most real tools you'll touch in a SOC actually run both engines at once, but it's worth understanding each one on its own first.

Signature-based detection matches traffic against a database of known attack patterns — a specific byte sequence in a packet's payload, or a particular exploit's fingerprint — the same basic idea as traditional antivirus matching a file against a list of known malware. It's fast and precise: when a signature-based rule fires, you can usually trust it, because it's matching something a vendor or researcher has already documented in detail. The tradeoff is that it's only ever as good as its signature database. An attack using a brand-new technique, with no matching signature written yet, sails straight through completely undetected, no matter how obviously malicious it would look to a human analyst.

Anomaly-based detection takes a different approach entirely. Instead of looking for a specific known pattern, it builds a baseline of what normal looks like for a given network or system — typical traffic volume, which protocols run at which times, how systems usually talk to each other — and then flags anything that deviates meaningfully from that baseline. Because it isn't tied to a documented signature, it can catch a genuinely novel, never-before-seen attack that a signature-based engine would miss entirely. The real cost is a higher false-positive rate: traffic that's legitimately unusual but completely harmless, like a one-time bulk data transfer, can trip the same alarm as an actual attacker.

That's exactly why most modern platforms, including Suricata, run both engines side by side. The signature engine handles known threats fast and with very few false alarms, while the anomaly engine watches everything else, including attacks nobody has documented yet. Running them together gives a SOC broad coverage without giving up the precision signatures provide on the threats that are already well understood.
Next, we'll get hands-on with the actual syntax: reading and writing a basic Snort or Suricata rule, line by line, so a real detection rule stops looking like an unreadable string of symbols.
